title: A study funded by NASA reveals that a Martian meteorite is one of the oldest ever found
excerpt: This 800-gram rock, discovered in the Sahara Desert in 2022, formed more than 4.1 billion years ago.
content:
A pink meteorite discovered in the Sahara Desert in 2022 originated on Mars and is more than 4.1 billion years old. Its age was determined by NASA-funded researchers who analyzed the minerals in the rock, which weighs approximately 800 grams.

A study published in the journal Science presents the first detailed analysis of Teghaza 001 and provides insights into the Martian crust during its earliest stages. Because it formed more than 4.1 billion years ago, the rock preserves evidence of geological processes that occurred on early Mars.

Another published study examined the meteorite's water content and provided clues about interactions between liquids and rocky materials during the early history of Mars. Together, these studies could help scientists understand how water altered the Martian crust.

Teghaza 001

The Teghaza 001 meteorite is one of the oldest Martian fragments ever found on Earth, dating back more than 4.1 billion years. Weighing approximately 800 grams, the rock contains an unusual combination of minerals formed as magma cooled inside the planet.

These characteristics make the sample an exceptional record of the formation of the Martian crust and the earliest geological processes on Mars.

Teghaza 001 preserves a mineralogical diversity that allows scientists to reconstruct different stages of its evolution. Its composition indicates that the crust formed as magmatic material cooled and was later modified through interactions with groundwater.

Discovery in the Sahara

The rock was discovered in 2022 in the Sahara Desert, in a region of Mali known as the Teghaza salt flats, from which it takes its name. The meteorite belongs to a group of approximately 435 recognised Martian fragments found on Earth and ranks among the three oldest ever identified.

Like other Martian meteorites, Teghaza 001 was ejected into space following a powerful impact on the planet's surface, traveled through interplanetary space, and eventually reached Earth. Its origin can be confirmed by comparing its mineral and chemical composition with data collected from Mars.

New clues about Mars

The composition of the Teghaza 001 meteorite has revealed important information about the formation of Mars' ancient crust. Among the features identified are minerals capable of preserving records of rock formation. The analysis revealed that the fragment formed more than 4.1 billion years ago.

To determine its age, the team used an in situ dating technique, analyzing individual mineral grains. Unlike conventional methods, which require dissolving the entire sample, this approach preserves nearly all the material for future studies and analyses.

Evidence of water on Mars

The analysis also revealed evidence that Teghaza 001 was altered by the presence of water on Mars approximately 4.1 billion years ago. Oxygen characteristics, texture, and chemical composition suggest that the water cycle on early Mars may have been more dynamic than previously thought.

This evidence helps scientists understand how water circulated and altered materials on the surface and within the Martian crust. Researchers hope that further analysis of Teghaza 001 will allow them to better reconstruct environmental conditions and understand how Mars lost some of its water over the course of its evolution.

Article reference

NASA. (2026). NASA-funded Study Details One of Oldest Mars Meteorites Ever Found.
